written.myAnswer: Artificial Intelligence is the ability of machines or computer systems to perform tasks that normally require human intelligence.

AI grew from early research into whether machines could think, including foundational work in the mid-20th century and the naming of the field at the 1956 Dartmouth workshop. It later advanced through periods of progress and reduced funding, and developed into modern data-driven systems such as machine learning and deep learning, now used in many fields.
Examples include automated diagnosis and remote patient monitoring.
AI techniques help machine-learning models identify patterns in data and improve their performance, including accuracy.
The Internet of Things is a network of physical devices connected to the internet that collect and exchange data.
IoT links devices and systems so they can communicate, collect and share data, enabling monitoring, coordination and automation.
Risks include security and privacy breaches, biased decisions, job displacement and lack of transparency.
AI and IoT can make daily services more connected, automated and personalized, while also raising concerns about privacy, security and employment.
Algorithmic bias is unfair or discriminatory output from an algorithm, often caused by biased data or methods and potentially reinforcing existing social biases.
Ethical principles help ensure AI and IoT are fair, transparent, accountable, secure and respectful of privacy and data rights.

AI can personalize learning by adapting lessons to a student's progress; intelligent tutoring systems can give individual guidance; automated assessment can mark quizzes and provide quick feedback; and AI tools can help teachers identify students who need support. These applications can make learning more tailored and help teachers use their time effectively.
Whitebox models have decision-making processes that people can understand; blackbox models produce decisions whose reasoning is difficult to understand.

An IoT system commonly includes sensors or devices to collect data, a network or gateway to transmit it, processing or cloud services to analyse it, and applications or actuators to present results or perform actions. Together these components collect, communicate and act on data.
Transportation uses of IoT include smart traffic management, Vehicle-to-Vehicle communication and predictive maintenance of vehicles.

IoT devices can collect sensitive information, enable tracking, or expose data through weak security or unclear data practices. Consent, data protection and user control help reduce these privacy risks.
AI and IoT automate some tasks and change roles and work environments. This may displace some workers while increasing demand for specialized skills and creating more connected workplaces.

Policies and regulations establish requirements for privacy, security, fairness and accountability. Examples include the EU General Data Protection Regulation and NIST guidance. They can help address risks, but their effectiveness depends on enforcement, compliance and keeping the rules up to date.

Algorithmic bias occurs when AI produces unfair outcomes, often perpetuating social biases, and can harm individuals or groups. Mitigation includes representative data, bias testing, transparency, human oversight and accountability.
Responsible AI and IoT should uphold fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, security, human oversight and respect for data rights throughout design and deployment.
